title: The Week That Was
gist: A weekly roundup of Lawfare's coverage spans Trump-administration legal battles (a DOJ memo authorizing military arrests near border 'national defense areas,' a D.C. special grand jury, Disney v. FCC, the Abrego Garcia case, a mail-in-ballot injunction), an analysis of the Iran war entering a 'bargaining phase' contingent on Strait of Hormuz control, and pieces on Lithuania-Belarus sanctions friction, Canada's CLOUD Act risk, Colombia's peace deal, and AI governance in courts and via a proposed Frontier AI Standards Body.

themes.theme: Trump Administration Legal and Institutional Battles

insights.claim: The Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel issued a new memorandum stating that the Posse Comitatus Act, which generally bars using the military for domestic law enforcement, does not prevent military personnel from making arrests near designated 'national defense areas,' such as portions of the U.S.-Mexico border.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A concrete legal reinterpretation expanding the military's domestic law-enforcement role at the border -- watch for expansion of 'national defense area' designations to other zones.
insights.locator: Peter Beck shared the Department of Justice's Office of Legal Counsel's new memorandum

insights.claim: A special grand jury has been empaneled in Washington, D.C. by Jeanine Pirro; analysis by Anna Bower argues that the special grand jury's defining feature -- its ability to issue public reports -- is subject to significant legal limitations that could prevent it from delivering the political win Pirro may be seeking.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Suggests high-profile special-grand-jury investigations under this administration may underdeliver politically due to procedural constraints on what they can publicly report.
insights.locator: Anna Bower discussed the inner workings of special grand juries

insights.claim: Federal law's structure around special grand juries means that turning one loose to investigate purported crimes can, on occasion, backfire on the prosecution itself.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A general risk model for prosecutors and observers: aggressive use of special grand juries for political cases carries a real chance of producing outcomes adverse to the prosecution.
insights.locator: Wittes and Bower discussed how special grand juries work

insights.claim: Disney is suing the Federal Communications Commission over its order requiring ABC-owned stations to file early license renewals, one of several active Trump-administration litigation fronts tracked this week alongside the Justice Department's appeal of the dismissal of Kilmar Abrego Garcia's criminal case.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A direct corporate-vs-regulator legal fight to track for FCC authority precedent over broadcast licensees; relevant to Disney/media regulatory risk.
insights.locator: Wittes sat down with Molly Roberts, Bower, and Eric Columbus

insights.claim: A nationwide preliminary injunction has been issued against President Trump's mail-in ballot executive order, and a new birthright citizenship order is also being litigated, alongside a case from a fired Justice Department prosecutor challenging his firing.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Multiple simultaneous executive-order challenges signal an active pattern of courts blocking or reviewing administration actions on elections and citizenship this cycle.
insights.locator: Wittes spoke with Roberts, Bower, and Roger Parloff

insights.claim: Discussion of the second Trump administration's purge of the National Security Council covered its institutional impacts and included the account of a trans former NSC staffer who says the administration badly needed her expertise but would not let her use the bathroom.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Illustrates how personnel/culture policy under the administration is affecting retention of specialized national-security expertise, a workforce-capacity risk for NSC functioning.
insights.locator: Julia Curlee to discuss articles she wrote in The Atlantic and Lawfare

insights.claim: A review of LGBT exclusion, subsequent inclusion, and renewed exclusion at the CIA highlighted the legal and cultural institutions that made greater acceptance possible historically, and argued those same institutions are under threat today.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Frames current personnel policy shifts at intelligence agencies as part of a cyclical institutional pattern rather than a one-off change -- relevant to workforce and morale risk at the CIA.
insights.locator: Trace Ballard, Curlee, and Todd Johannessen reviewed the history of LGBT exclusion

themes.theme: Iran War Bargaining Phase and Nuclear Escalation Risk

insights.claim: The war with Iran has entered a 'bargaining phase' in which the parties use military force and diplomacy in tandem to pursue a favorable negotiated settlement, according to analysis by Curlee and Tabatabai.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Signals the Iran conflict is shifting from pure military confrontation toward a hybrid force-and-negotiation phase -- relevant for assessing near-term escalation vs. de-escalation risk in Gulf energy markets.
insights.locator: Curlee and Ariane Tabatabai explained that the war with Iran has entered a bargaining phase

insights.claim: A durable end to the Iran war depends on three factors combining together: clarity on who controls the Strait of Hormuz, each side's leadership being able to sell a deal domestically, and the potential for allied parties on either side to act as spoilers -- a deal must address all three to hold.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Strait of Hormuz control clarity is a named precondition for a durable settlement -- a key variable to watch for oil-shipping and energy-market risk given the strait's role in global crude flows.
insights.locator: Curlee and Ariane Tabatabai explained that the war with Iran has entered a bargaining phase

insights.claim: Preventing nuclear escalation among the three nuclear great powers -- the U.S., Russia, and China -- depends on the U.S. correctly understanding its adversaries' nuclear first-use posture and anticipating how its own posture could be misread, since each country's approach to first use is prone to misinterpretation, per Fiona Cunningham and Kristin Ven Bruusgaard.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Frames nuclear-escalation risk among the three great powers as primarily a signaling/misinterpretation problem rather than a capability problem -- relevant to how markets should price tail nuclear risk during crises.
insights.locator: Fiona Cunningham and Kristin Ven Bruusgaard discussed the conditions

insights.claim: U.S. pressure over Lithuania's enforcement of EU sanctions on potash exports from Belarus is forcing Lithuania to choose between appeasing the United States, its key security partner, and avoiding actions that would strengthen Belarus, a Russian ally on its border -- a dynamic that sidesteps the EU in the dispute, per Katsiaryna Shmatsina's analysis.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A bilateral U.S.-Lithuania sanctions dispute over Belarusian potash is bypassing EU sanctions coordination -- worth watching for fragmentation of EU sanctions unity and potash/fertilizer trade flow disruption.
insights.locator: Katsiaryna Shmatsina analyzed the mounting tensions between the United States and Lithuania

insights.claim: Canada's proposed Bill C-22, which would compel U.S. companies to build law-enforcement surveillance capabilities into their products for Canadian authorities, risks alienating the cybersecurity-focused U.S. government and could jeopardize Canada's chances of securing a CLOUD Act agreement that would give it more stable access to cross-border evidence, according to Richard Salgado.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A concrete example of domestic surveillance-mandate legislation creating friction with U.S. cross-border data-sharing deals -- relevant for tech companies operating in Canada and for CLOUD Act negotiation risk more broadly.
insights.locator: Richard Salgado argued that Canada's proposed Bill C-22

insights.claim: Newly elected Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella's attacks on the country's 2016 peace deal are constrained because its core provisions are anchored in Congress and the Constitutional Court, making outright repeal difficult, but he could still erode the deal's implementation at the edges, undermining its credibility for other armed groups weighing deals of their own, per Isabel Rowan Scarpino's analysis.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Colombia's peace framework is structurally resilient to outright repeal but vulnerable to slow erosion -- a signal for assessing continued conflict/demobilization risk with other armed groups.
insights.locator: Isabel Rowan Scarpino discussed newly elected Colombian President

insights.claim: Technology companies whose infrastructure -- such as data centers -- has both civilian and military applications face a range of legal threats when operating in conflict zones, and while international humanitarian law leaves key questions unclear, contract law may provide companies with additional protections, per Adam Hickey, Veronica Glick, Rohith George, and Rachael O'Grady.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Flags legal exposure for data-center and cloud-infrastructure operators with dual-use assets in or near conflict zones, and points to contract law as an underused risk-mitigation lever.
insights.locator: Adam Hickey, Veronica Glick, Rohith George, and Rachael O'Grady explained

insights.claim: The Trump administration released a National Security Science & Technology Strategy intended to support its 2025 National Security Strategy by prioritizing U.S. leadership in emerging technology development.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A formal administration document tying national security policy to emerging-tech leadership -- relevant for tracking federal R&D and tech-sector priorities tied to national security funding.
insights.locator: Sarah Willrich shared the Trump administration's National Security Science & Technology Strategy

insights.claim: Courts should adopt a controlled AI 'playground' to explore using AI for judicial analysis while managing risks like hallucinations and AI-driven scope drift from users' intentions, rather than avoiding AI entirely or deploying it unchecked, according to Daniel Ho and Olivia Martin.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Proposes a sandboxed-adoption model for judicial AI use that vendors selling legal-AI tools to courts could align product design toward.
insights.locator: Daniel E. Ho and Olivia H. Martin considered how artificial intelligence

insights.claim: A discussion of a proposed U.S.-led Frontier AI Standards Body weighed a FINRA-like self-regulatory model, considering both the benefits for public trust and the risk that allied nations may be reluctant to accept a U.S.-based body as the international AI standard-setter.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A FINRA-style self-regulatory body for frontier AI is being actively floated -- relevant to AI labs and investors tracking the direction of U.S. AI regulation and international standard-setting fragmentation risk.
insights.locator: Kate Klonick was joined by Vinh Nguyen, Elham Tabassi, and Kat Duffy

insights.claim: A discussion explored AI's impact on the collapse of institutional trust and the relationship between AI, information integrity, labor disruption, institutional legitimacy, and democratic resilience.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Positions AI-driven institutional trust erosion as a named, actively studied risk category linking AI deployment to labor markets and democratic stability.
insights.locator: Matt Abrams joined Kevin Frazier to explore the impact of AI
